title: How to Invest During a Recession

seo.seoTitle: How to Invest During a Recession
seo.metaDescription: A recession doesn't mean you should stop investing. Here's a level-headed approach to protecting your portfolio and finding opportunity during economic downturns.
seo.focusKeyword: how to invest during a recession
secondaryKeywords: what to do with stocks in a downturn
seo.searchIntent: Informational — investors seeking guidance during or in anticipation of an economic downturn.

excerpt: Recessions are a normal part of the economic cycle. Historically, the biggest investing mistake during one isn't holding stocks — it's panic-selling near the bottom.
intro: Recessions are an uncomfortable but historically normal part of the economic cycle, and they tend to trigger the same instinct in most investors: sell everything and wait for things to calm down. That instinct, while understandable, has historically been one of the most costly mistakes an investor can make, because it converts a temporary paper loss into a permanent, realized one. Here's a more level-headed framework for navigating a downturn.

sections.heading: Understand That Downturns Are Temporary by Design
paragraphs: Every recession in modern market history has eventually been followed by a recovery, though the length of that recovery varies. Stock prices are forward-looking, which means markets often begin recovering well before the underlying economic data actually improves, since investors are pricing in an eventual recovery ahead of time. This is part of why trying to time an exact bottom is so difficult — by the time economic news feels reassuring again, much of the market recovery may have already happened.

sections.heading: Resist the Urge to Sell Everything
paragraphs: Selling during a downturn locks in your losses and removes any chance of participating in the eventual recovery. Unless your financial situation has genuinely changed — job loss, an urgent need for cash — maintaining your existing long-term positions through a downturn has historically served investors better than exiting and trying to re-enter later, an approach that requires being right twice: correctly timing the exit and correctly timing the re-entry.

callout.title: Selling low is the actual risk, not the downturn itself
callout.text: A stock decline only becomes a permanent loss if you sell. As long as the underlying business remains sound, a temporary price drop is a paper loss, not a realized one.

sections.heading: Consider Continuing to Invest, If You Can
paragraphs: For investors still contributing regularly, a recession means new contributions are buying shares at lower prices than before — the same [dollar-cost averaging](/financial-intelligence/what-is-dollar-cost-averaging) principle that applies in any market environment. This doesn't mean trying to guess the exact bottom; it means continuing your existing contribution schedule rather than pausing out of fear, if your personal financial situation allows it.

sections.heading: Revisit Your Risk Tolerance and Diversification
paragraphs: A recession is a genuinely useful moment to honestly assess whether your portfolio's risk level matches your actual tolerance and timeline — if a downturn is causing you significant stress or you're seriously considering selling everything, that's valuable information for adjusting your allocation once markets stabilize, not during the peak of the panic. This is also a good time to confirm your holdings are appropriately diversified across [both growth and value](/financial-intelligence/growth-stocks-vs-value-stocks) exposure and different company sizes, since concentration in a single volatile category tends to amplify recession-era stress.

keyTakeaways: Recessions are a historically normal, temporary part of the economic cycle, and markets often recover before economic data itself improves.
Selling during a downturn converts a temporary paper loss into a permanent, realized one.
Trying to time an exact bottom requires being right about both the exit and the re-entry — a very difficult combination.
Continuing regular contributions during a downturn, if your finances allow, buys shares at lower average prices over time.
Use the emotional discomfort of a downturn as information about your true risk tolerance for future allocation decisions, not as a signal to sell at the worst time.

faq.question: Should I stop investing during a recession?
faq.answer: For most long-term investors with a stable financial situation, continuing regular contributions through a downturn has historically been more effective than stopping, since it takes advantage of lower average purchase prices over time.

faq.question: What sectors tend to hold up better during a recession?
faq.answer: Consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare have historically shown more resilience during downturns since demand for essentials tends to stay more stable, though no sector is entirely immune to a broad economic decline.

faq.question: Is it a good idea to move everything to cash during a recession?
faq.answer: Moving entirely to cash locks in losses and requires correctly timing re-entry to benefit from the eventual recovery — a difficult combination that has historically underperformed simply staying invested for most long-term investors.

conclusion: The most damaging recession-era mistake isn't holding stocks through a decline — it's abandoning a sound long-term plan out of short-term fear. Stay diversified, keep contributing if your finances allow it, and remember that recessions have historically been temporary chapters in a much longer investing story, not the end of it.
